title: Ratio & Proportion Applied
subtitle: Rates, scale drawings, and the questions the exam actually asks.
objectives: Distinguish a ratio from a rate
Use a unit rate to solve a proportion problem
Read and use a scale on a map or drawing
Decide when two quantities are in direct proportion
Review the whole ratio topic for the exam

cards.title: A ratio with units attached has its own name
cards.text: Three to four is a ratio. Ninety pesos per kilogram is a rate. The difference is whether the two things are measured in the same unit.

cards.title: Ratio, rate, unit rate
cards.text: All three compare two quantities. What changes is whether the units match and whether one side is exactly one.
points: **Ratio** — same units. 3 boys to 4 girls.
**Rate** — different units. 180 km in 3 hours.
**Unit rate** — one side is exactly 1. 60 km per hour.
**A unit rate is always a division.**

question.text: Which of these is a RATE rather than a ratio?
question.explain: Different units, kilometres against hours. The other three compare like with like.

cards.title: Find one, then multiply
cards.text: Almost every proportion word problem can be solved without cross-multiplication if you find the value of one first.
points: **5 books cost ₱400** → one book is ₱80.
**Divide to find one. Multiply to find many.**
**Slower to write, much harder to get wrong.**

cards.title: Fuel per lap is the unit rate that decides a race
cards.text: Work out litres per lap and you know how many laps a tank gives you. Get it wrong and you stop on the last corner.
points: **45 litres over 25 laps** → 1.8 litres per lap.
**A 60-litre tank** → 60 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 33 laps.
**One division each way.**
**Race engineers do this constantly.**

question.text: 6 identical pens cost ₱90. What do 10 cost?

cards.title: A scale is a ratio between drawing and reality
cards.text: A scale of 1 : 100 means one centimetre on the paper is one hundred centimetres in real life.
points: **Scale 1 : 100** — the drawing is 100 times smaller.
**Drawing to real:** multiply by the scale.
**Real to drawing:** divide by the scale.
**Keep the units the same** on both sides.

cards.title: Every map you have ever opened has a scale
cards.text: The minimap is the world divided by a fixed number. That number is a ratio, and it never changes as you move.
points: **Zoom changes the scale**, not the world.
**A scale bar** tells you what one screen unit means.
**Same maths as a paper map.**
**A model car at 1 : 64** is the same idea again.

question.text: A map has a scale of 1 : 50000. A road measures 4 cm. How long is it really?
question.explain: 4 × 50000 = 200000 cm. That is 2000 m, which is 2 km.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Rates and scale done. Part 2 is when proportion applies, and when it does not. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Not everything scales, and the exam knows it
cards.text: Twice the flour makes twice the bread. Twice the workers does not always halve the time, and neither does twice the runners.

cards.title: Double one, double the other
cards.text: Two quantities are in direct proportion when multiplying one by any number multiplies the other by the same number.
points: **Cost and quantity** — buy twice as many, pay twice.
**Distance and time** at a steady speed.
**Ingredients in a recipe.**
**Divide one by the other** and you get the same number.

cards.title: Things that look proportional and are not
cards.text: The exam sets these deliberately, and they are worth recognising rather than calculating.
points: **Age** — twice as old in ten years is nonsense.
**A race time** does not halve if you train twice as long.
**Nine women** cannot make a baby in one month.
**Ask whether doubling really doubles it.**

cards.title: Training does not scale proportionally
cards.text: Doubling the hours does not double the result. Recovery is part of the process, and there is a limit to how much fits in a week.
points: **Some things scale.** Rounds per session, roughly.
**Most do not.** Progress, recovery, sleep need.
**Assuming everything is proportional** is the error.
**It is also a real training mistake.**

question.text: Which pair is in direct proportion?
options: Number of tickets and total cost
Runners in a race and the winning time
question.explain: Twice the tickets is exactly twice the cost. None of the other three scale that cleanly.

cards.title: The whole topic in four moves
cards.text: Every ratio question in the exam is one of these four, or a combination of two.
points: **Simplify** — divide both sides by the same number.
**Find the missing term** — cross-multiply.
**Share an amount** — add parts, find one, multiply.
**Scale up or down** — find the unit rate first.

question.text: A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of rice. How much for 10 people?
question.explain: One person needs 300 ÷ 4 = 75 g. Then 10 × 75 = 750 g.

terms.def: A comparison of two quantities with different units, such as km per hour.
A rate where one side is exactly one. Always found by dividing.
The ratio between a drawing and the real thing, such as 1 : 50000.
Multiply one quantity by any number and the other multiplies by the same.
Multiplying diagonally across a proportion to find a missing term.
The number you multiply by to go from the drawing to the real size.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Ratio: same units. Rate: different units.**
**Find one, then multiply.** It rarely goes wrong.
**Scale 1 : n means multiply the drawing by n.**
**Ask whether doubling really doubles it.**

quiz.text: Which of these is a rate?
quiz.explain: Pesos and kilograms are different units, which is what makes it a rate rather than a ratio.
quiz.objective: Distinguish a ratio from a rate

quiz.text: A car travels 240 km in 4 hours. What is the unit rate?
quiz.explain: 240 ÷ 4 = 60. A unit rate has exactly one on one side.
quiz.objective: Distinguish a ratio from a rate

quiz.text: 8 identical sandbags cost ₱200. What do 14 cost?
quiz.objective: Use a unit rate to solve a proportion problem

quiz.text: A machine makes 150 parts in 5 minutes. How many in 12 minutes?
quiz.objective: Use a unit rate to solve a proportion problem

quiz.text: A model car is built at 1 : 24 and measures 18 cm. How long is the real car?
quiz.explain: 18 x 24 = 432 cm, which is 4.32 m. About the length of a real car, so the answer is sane.
quiz.objective: Read and use a scale on a map or drawing

quiz.text: On an evacuation map at 1 : 25 000, the shelter is 8 cm away. How far is that really?
quiz.objective: Read and use a scale on a map or drawing

quiz.text: A real car is 4 m long. A model is 1 : 64 scale. How long is the model?
quiz.explain: 4 m is 400 cm. 400 ÷ 64 = 6.25 cm. Real to drawing means dividing.
quiz.objective: Read and use a scale on a map or drawing

quiz.text: A relief pack for 6 people uses 450 g of rice. How much for 8 people?
Which pair is in direct proportion?
options: Litres of petrol and the cost of filling up
A person's age and their shoe size
The number of players and the length of a match
Hours of sleep and marks in an exam
quiz.explain: Twice the litres is exactly twice the cost. The other three do not scale cleanly at all.
quiz.objective: Decide when two quantities are in direct proportion

quiz.text: Double a meteor’s speed and its energy doubles.
quiz.explain: Energy is half m v squared. Double the mass and energy doubles; double the speed and it quadruples.
quiz.objective: Decide when two quantities are in direct proportion

teacher.summary: Week 10 Math applies ratio and proportion and reviews the topic before the exam. Two things get more weight than usual. The first is the find-one-then-multiply method, which is slower to write than cross-multiplication and far harder to get wrong, and is therefore the better default under exam pressure. The second is the section on quantities that are not in direct proportion: the exam sets those deliberately, and the useful skill is recognising them rather than calculating them. The training card makes the same point in a domain he cares about, where assuming everything scales is a real and common mistake rather than a maths-lesson abstraction.
discussion: Ask him to solve a proportion two ways, by cross-multiplying and by finding one. Both work; one is easier to check.
Ask what scale his model cars are and what that number means. 1 : 64 stops being decoration.
Ask him to name three things that are not in direct proportion. It is harder than it sounds.
Ask whether training twice as long makes you twice as good. He already knows the answer, and now it has a name.
teacher.extension: Give him a floor plan or a map with a scale and have him work out two real distances. Then have him measure one of them and check.
misconceptions: 'Ratio and rate are the same word.' A rate compares different units. A ratio compares like with like.
'A scale of 1 : 100 means the drawing is 100 times bigger.' It is 100 times smaller. The real thing is bigger.
'Everything scales in proportion.' Age, race times and workers per job do not. The exam relies on that error.
'Cross-multiplication is the only method.' Finding the unit rate first works for nearly every word problem and is easier to check.
